855.title: The first split
855.hook: the Sthaviras and the Mahasanghikas part ways; accounts differ on why
855.howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists trace their lineage through the Sthavira side; East Asian and Tibetan monastic lineages keep Vinaya codes that come from other early schools.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yasa at Vesali, coins in a bowl and salt in a horn. Your line: the ten points. Today, the community divides.

Two communities of monks. Both shave their heads, both wear the robe, both recite the Buddha's words and keep a code of discipline. At some point in the generations after the Buddha, they stop meeting together for the observance day. One side becomes known as the Sthaviras, the elders. The other as the Mahasanghikas, the great community. Ask why, and you get more than one answer, depending on whose books you open.
screen: `TWO COMMUNITIES OF MONKS.` → `THE ELDERS, THE GREAT COMMUNITY.` → `MORE THAN ONE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: The Dipavamsa, a chronicle kept in the Theravada tradition, ties the split to Vesali. The monks who lost over the ten points, it says, didn't accept the verdict. They held a great council of their own and arranged the texts their own way, and from that great assembly came the name Mahasanghika. Texts preserved in northern traditions, such as a treatise on the schools attributed to Vasumitra, tell it differently. There the quarrel is over points about the arahant, the fully awakened one: could such a person still have doubts, or not know some things, or need others to tell him he was awakened? On this telling the split was over what awakening is, not over salt and coins. Some modern scholars point to yet another text that suggests the elders wanted to add rules to the discipline, and the larger group refused. If that's right, the side called the great community was the one keeping the old rules unchanged. None of the three can be checked from outside; the old texts each come from a school with its own memory, and the modern reading rests on one more such text. The Dipavamsa, from the Sthavira line, remembers its side as keeping faith with Vesali. The northern treatises remember a quarrel about awakening. You don't have to choose a side to learn from this. The first split teaches a habit: when a story about a division is told, ask who is telling it.

Your line: accounts differ. Each side remembers the split in its own way. Until tomorrow.

856.title: Eighteen schools
856.hook: the early schools multiplied, each with its own reading of the texts
856.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics today are ordained in lineages whose discipline codes trace back to particular early schools, and students of Buddhism read the early schools' debates in texts like the Kathavatthu.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Sthaviras and the great community, and three stories of why they parted. Your line: accounts differ. Today, the branches keep branching.

Eighteen. That's the number the old chronicles give for the schools that grew up after the first split. The trouble is, when you put the lists side by side, they don't name the same eighteen. Some lists have more names than that. Some schools appear under two names. The number stays the same while the names shift around it, as if eighteen were less a count than a way of saying: a whole family of schools.
screen: `EIGHTEEN, SAY THE CHRONICLES.` → `THE LISTS DON'T MATCH.` → `A WHOLE FAMILY OF SCHOOLS.`

segments.voice: These weren't separate religions. A school, a nikaya, was a community of monks with its own lineage, its own copy of the discipline, and often its own way of reading the teaching. A few of the readings: the Sarvastivada taught that all things exist in the past, present and future, and their name is read as those who say all exists. Another family of schools, the Pudgalavadins, held that there is a person, a pudgala, which is neither the same as the parts of body and mind nor separate from them. The Lokottaravada, a branch of the great community, taught that the Buddha's life in the world was in a deep sense beyond the world. The Theravada called itself the teaching of the elders. How did they argue? The Theravada canon even contains a book, the Kathavatthu, that sets out points of controversy as question and answer: a position is stated, questioned, and answered. It is written from the Theravada side, but it preserves the questions other schools were asking. Today the Theravada continues as a living school with its canon in Pali, and the discipline codes of other early schools still guide monks and nuns in East Asia and Tibet. Each of these schools kept faith with the texts the way its teachers had, and each, the Theravada included, understood itself as keeping the Buddha's teaching whole.

857.title: Ashoka's remorse
857.hook: the emperor conquers Kalinga, sees the slaughter, and repents (Rock Edict 13)
857.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell the story of Ashoka after Kalinga as an example of a ruler who turned from conquest to dhamma, and the edict is read today as a public act of regret.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the eighteen schools, one teaching read many ways. Your line: many readings.

Kings carve their victories into rock. This one carved a regret. In a long inscription, cut by royal order where passersby could find it, a ruler who calls himself Beloved of the Gods looks back at the war that made him master of a land called Kalinga. He does not boast. He counts: the killed, the carried away, the ones who died afterward. And then, in public stone, he says he is grieved. Scholars call it Rock Edict Thirteen. Buddhists remember the man as Ashoka.
screen: `A KING CARVES A REGRET.` → `HE COUNTS THE COST.` → `HE SAYS HE IS GRIEVED.`

segments.voice: First, the war, counted in stone. Kalinga was conquered, the edict says, and great numbers of people were killed, or died, or were taken from their homes. The king puts the figures in his own inscription. Second, whose suffering weighed on him. Not only soldiers: priests and wandering ascetics, householders who listened to their mothers and fathers, honored their teachers, and were kind to friends, relatives and servants. They were hurt, killed, or torn from the people they loved. Even those who escaped unharmed, the edict says, grieved for friends who didn't. This weighs on the king heavily. Third, the turn. After Kalinga, his devotion to dhamma grew: to the good way of living, to care, to restraint. He calls conquest by dhamma the best conquest, and asks his sons and grandsons not to seek new conquests, or, if they must conquer, to choose patience and light punishment. Fourth, the regret made public. He could have kept it in his heart; he put it where strangers would read it. A Buddhist sutta sits beside it. King Ajatasattu confesses to the Buddha that he killed his own father. The Buddha doesn't excuse it. He says that seeing a wrong as a wrong, owning it, and restraining yourself after is growth in the discipline of the noble ones. Regret isn't the end of the story; it's where the turning starts. The edict doesn't bring back anyone from Kalinga, and doesn't pretend to. It just refuses to call the war glorious.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you did that you'd take back, not the worst thing in your life, just one real one, and look at it the way the edict looks at Kalinga: what happened, and who it touched. No excuses, and no beating yourself up either. Then ask quietly what restraint or small amends might follow, and let the question rest with the breath.

Your line: the conqueror repents. Seeing a wrong as a wrong is where the turning starts. Day eight hundred fifty-seven, done.

858.title: Ashoka's edicts
858.hook: carved in stone across India: honor other people's faiths as well as your own (Rock Edict 12)
858.howItsDone: Buddhists and historians point to Ashoka's twelfth rock edict as a public call for respect between religious communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ashoka's remorse, a king who counted his war's cost in stone. Your line: the conqueror repents.

No printing press, no screens, no post. How does a king talk to everyone at once? Ashoka chose rock. He had his words cut into boulders and polished stone pillars where people passed, and some readers picture someone who could read reading them out to those who couldn't. The messages weren't lists of taxes. They were about how to live. And one, the edict scholars number twelve, takes on a question that still starts arguments at dinner tables: how should people of one faith speak about another?
screen: `NO PRESS, NO POST.` → `WORDS CUT INTO ROCK.` → `HOW TO SPEAK OF ANOTHER FAITH.`

segments.voice: First, written to last. The edicts speak in the king's own voice, Beloved of the Gods, and say plainly they were written so the teaching of dhamma would endure. They're not scripture; they're a ruler's public letters about kindness, honesty and care. Second, the root. Rock Edict Twelve says the king honors all the religious communities, wandering ascetics and householders, with gifts and respect. But he values something more than gifts: that the essential part of every one of them should grow. The root of that growth is restraint in speech. Don't praise your own community and run down another's without reason, and when there is reason, do it lightly. Third, the surprise. Whoever praises their own faith and condemns another's, just to make their own look good, the edict says, does their own community more harm. Honoring the other faith helps your own; running it down injures it. Fourth, listening. Concord is good, the edict says: people should hear one another's teaching and become well informed. The king wants communities that know each other, not just tolerate each other from a distance. Buddhist tradition remembers Ashoka as a patron of the sangha, yet here, in public stone, he asks respect for every community in his lands. It's a king's instruction, and it reads like advice for a group chat.

859.title: Wells and hospitals
859.hook: the edicts list shade trees, wells, and medicine for people and animals (Rock Edict 2)
859.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers hold up Ashoka's public works as an example of generosity in practice, and the Vinaya story of the sick monk makes tending the sick part of monastic life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ashoka's edicts, and the call to honor other faiths. Your line: carved in stone.

Midday on a dusty road. A trader leading an ox, a mother with a child on her hip, a stray dog with its tongue out, all looking for the same two things: water and shade. You might expect a royal inscription to list palaces and victories. Ashoka's second rock edict lists something smaller and stranger: medicine, herbs, wells, trees along the road. And it says, more than once, that these are for people and for animals alike.
screen: `A HOT ROAD.` → `WATER AND SHADE.` → `FOR PEOPLE AND FOR ANIMALS.`

segments.voice: First, care for two kinds of patient. Rock Edict Two says the king arranged medical care for people and for animals; translators give treatment, or care. Whether there were hospital buildings, the stone doesn't say, and it's honest to leave it there. Second, herbs where there were none. Where healing plants, roots and fruits didn't grow, they were brought in and planted, and not only in his own lands: the edict says this reached neighboring kingdoms too. Third, the road. Wells were dug and trees planted along the roads, for people and animals. A pillar inscription fills in the picture: banyans for shade, mango groves, wells, rest houses, places for animals to drink. Who benefits from a shade tree? Not the king, and usually not the person who plants it. Whoever walks by, years from now, on a hot afternoon. Fourth, why a Buddhist king would care. The Vinaya, the monastic rulebook, tells of a monk lying sick in his own filth, with no one tending him. The Buddha and Ananda wash him and lay him down. Then the Buddha tells the monks, in effect: you have no mother and father here; if you don't care for one another, who will? Whoever would tend the Buddha, he says, should tend the sick. The edict doesn't mention that story, but they share an instinct: care that doesn't ask who deserves it, even for the dog on the road.

860.title: The third council
860.hook: the Theravada chronicles place a council at Pataliputta under Ashoka
860.howItsDone: In Theravada countries the council at Pataliputta is counted among the great councils that preserved the teaching, and the elder Moggaliputta Tissa is remembered as its leader.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the edict on wells and medicine, care for people and animals alike. Your line: shade for travelers.

In a monastery in the capital, the monks have stopped meeting. On the observance days, when they should gather to recite the rules together, they stay apart, because they no longer trust who among them is really a monk. The chronicles of Sri Lanka say outsiders had put on robes for the food and the honor, and brought their own teachings with them. The king sends a minister to set things right. In the chronicle's telling, it goes badly wrong.
screen: `THE MONKS STOP MEETING.` → `WHO IS REALLY A MONK?` → `THE KING SENDS A MINISTER.`

segments.voice: First, the order gone wrong. The minister, the Mahavamsa says, misunderstands his instructions. When the monks still refuse to hold the observance with the others, he draws his sword and kills some of them, until the king's own brother, a monk, steps in front of the blade. Ashoka is horrified: is the guilt mine? Second, the elder's answer. The king sends for a senior monk, Moggaliputta Tissa, who tells him that without the intention, there is no guilt in the deed. Elsewhere the Buddha says it is intention he calls action; here that teaching meets a frightened king. Third, the question. The elder and the king sit together, the chronicle says, and each monk is asked one thing: what did the Buddha teach? Those who answer that he taught by analysis, taking things apart and looking, are kept; the others are sent away. Then the community recites the teaching together, and the elder sets out a book that answers wrong views point by point. Fourth, whose memory this is. This council is told in the Theravada chronicles kept in Sri Lanka, the Dipavamsa and the Mahavamsa. Other Buddhist schools tell Ashoka's time differently, and some place councils elsewhere. That isn't a scandal; every family remembers its own story. So today's line is careful: not that it happened just so, but that the chronicles remember. And it matters to the Theravada world, because the chronicle goes on to tell of teachers sent out from that council to other lands. Tomorrow, one of them crosses the sea.
screen: `A KING'S ORDER GOES WRONG.` · `NO INTENTION, NO GUILT.` · `WHAT DID THE BUDDHA TEACH?` · `THE CHRONICLES REMEMBER.`

861.title: Mahinda to Sri Lanka
861.hook: Ashoka's son Mahinda brings the teaching to the island (Mahavamsa 14)
861.howItsDone: Sri Lankan Buddhists remember Mahinda's arrival each year at the Poson full moon, when pilgrims climb the hill of Mihintale, where tradition places the meeting with the king.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Moggaliputta Tissa's council, as the Theravada chronicles tell it. Your line: the chronicles remember. Today ends the week, with a journey.

A king is hunting on a mountain, chasing a deer through the trees, bow in hand, his men somewhere behind him. Then a voice calls him by name. He turns, and on the rock above him stands a monk in robes, calm, unarmed, waiting. The king is Devanampiya Tissa, ruler of the island of Lanka. The monk, the Mahavamsa says, is Mahinda, son of the emperor Ashoka. The deer is gone. The conversation is about to begin.
screen: `A KING HUNTING A DEER.` → `A VOICE CALLS HIS NAME.` → `A MONK ON THE ROCK.`

segments.voice: First, the test. Before he teaches anything, Mahinda checks whether the king can think. He points to a tree. What is this called? A mango. Are there other mangoes besides this one? Many. And besides this mango and the other mangoes, are there other trees? Many, but they aren't mangoes. And besides the other mangoes and the trees that aren't mangoes, is there another? Yes, says the king: this mango tree. Then the same about relatives, and the king answers: besides my kin and those who aren't my kin, there's myself. The chronicle says Mahinda saw the king was sharp, and ready. Second, the teaching. Mahinda preaches a discourse there on the mountain, and the king takes refuge with the people around him. Third, a son of an emperor. In the chronicle, Mahinda had left a prince's life to become a monk, and was sent out after the council at Pataliputta. Tradition says Ashoka's own children carried the teaching to the island. However historians weigh the chronicle, in its telling this meeting is where the island's Buddhist story begins. Fourth, the week behind us. A split, the Sthaviras and the Mahasanghikas, and accounts that differ. Eighteen schools and many readings. Ashoka's remorse, carved in stone. His edicts asking respect for every faith. Wells, medicine and shade. A council the chronicles remember. And now a monk on a rock, and a teaching that has crossed the sea.
screen: `THE MANGO RIDDLE.` · `A TEACHING ON THE MOUNTAIN.` · `A SON OF ASHOKA.` · `THIS WEEK: FROM SPLIT TO SEA.`

segments.voice: Think back to how whatever you hold most deeply first reached you, a faith, a practice, a way of being kind, a love of quiet, and let one face come to mind: a grandparent, a teacher, a friend, a stranger, a book someone left lying around. Hold them with gratitude for a few breaths, whether they're near, far, or gone.
